Combinations of Capacitors

Real circuits combine capacitors to reach values and voltage ratings that no single component provides. Two questions settle every combination: which quantity is shared, and which one adds.

Parallel Combination

Capacitors are in parallel when the same \(\Delta V\) appears across each. Both top plates connect to one node, both bottom plates to another, so each capacitor sees the same two potentials.

Shared \(\Delta V\); the charges add:

\[Q_{\text{tot}} = Q_1 + Q_2 = C_1\Delta V + C_2\Delta V = (C_1 + C_2)\Delta V\]

\[\boxed{\;C_{\text{eq}} = C_1 + C_2 + C_3 + \cdots \qquad (\text{parallel})\;}\]

Parallel capacitors behave as one capacitor with more plate area. \(C_{\text{eq}}\) is always larger than the largest capacitor in the group.

Series Combination

Capacitors are in series when connected end to end, so that the same charge \(Q\) appears on each.

Why series capacitors must carry equal charge, and it is not an assumption. The conductor between two series capacitors — the bottom plate of the first joined to the top plate of the second — is electrically isolated. No wire reaches it from the battery. Whatever charge the battery pushes onto the first capacitor’s top plate induces an equal and opposite charge on the plate facing it, and the charge displaced from that plate has nowhere to go but the next capacitor. The isolated middle conductor started neutral and must stay neutral, which forces \(Q\) to be identical all the way along.

Shared \(Q\); the voltages add:

\[\Delta V_{\text{tot}} = \Delta V_1 + \Delta V_2 = \frac{Q}{C_1} + \frac{Q}{C_2} = Q\left(\frac{1}{C_1} + \frac{1}{C_2}\right)\]

\[\boxed{\;\frac{1}{C_{\text{eq}}} = \frac{1}{C_1} + \frac{1}{C_2} + \frac{1}{C_3} + \cdots \qquad (\text{series})\;}\]

Series capacitors behave as one capacitor with a larger plate separation. \(C_{\text{eq}}\) is always smaller than the smallest capacitor in the group.

Series and Parallel at a Glance

Property Parallel Series
Shared quantity \(\Delta V\) \(Q\)
Additive quantity \(Q_{\text{tot}} = Q_1 + Q_2\) \(\Delta V_{\text{tot}} = \Delta V_1 + \Delta V_2\)
Combination rule \(C_{\text{eq}} = C_1 + C_2\) \(1/C_{\text{eq}} = 1/C_1 + 1/C_2\)
Effect larger than any one smaller than any one
Physical picture more area more separation

These are the spring rules from Physics I, not the resistor rules. Springs in parallel share a displacement and their stiffnesses add, \(k_{\text{eq}} = k_1 + k_2\) — exactly the parallel-capacitor rule. Springs in series share a force and their compliances add, \(1/k_{\text{eq}} = 1/k_1 + 1/k_2\) — exactly the series-capacitor rule.

The correspondence runs \(C \leftrightarrow k\), \(\Delta V \leftrightarrow x\), \(Q \leftrightarrow F\), and §25.5 will show it extends to the stored energy.

Resistors, in Chapter 27, combine the opposite way — series resistances add. That reversal catches people every term, and the reason is worth carrying: it is \(C\) that adds in parallel because \(C\) measures capacity, while \(R\) measures opposition.

A Mixed Combination

\(C_1 = 4.00\ \mu\)F and \(C_2 = 6.00\ \mu\)F in series; that pair in parallel with \(C_4 = 8.00\ \mu\)F; the whole group in series with \(C_3 = 2.00\ \mu\)F, across \(\Delta V = 12.0\) V.

Work from the inside out. There is no formula for a network; there is only repeated application of the two rules to the innermost group that is purely series or purely parallel.

Step 1 — \(C_1\) and \(C_2\) in series:

\[\frac{1}{C_{12}} = \frac{1}{4.00} + \frac{1}{6.00} = \frac{5}{12} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad C_{12} = 2.40\ \mu\text{F}\]

Step 2 — that pair in parallel with \(C_4\):

\[C_{124} = C_{12} + C_4 = 2.40 + 8.00 = 10.4\ \mu\text{F}\]

Step 3 — the group in series with \(C_3\):

\[\frac{1}{C_{\text{eq}}} = \frac{1}{10.4} + \frac{1}{2.00} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad C_{\text{eq}} = 1.68\ \mu\text{F}\]

\[\boxed{\;C_{\text{eq}} = 1.68\ \mu\text{F}\;}\]

Check it against the bounds before trusting it. The last operation was a series combination with \(C_3 = 2.00\ \mu\)F, so the answer must come out smaller than \(2.00\ \mu\)F — and \(1.68\) is. Step 2 was a parallel combination, so \(10.4\) had to exceed \(8.00\) — it does. Step 1 was series, so \(2.40\) had to fall below \(4.00\) — it does.

Every step of a network reduction has a one-line sanity check available. Using them catches the single most common error in this material: applying the series rule to a parallel pair, or the reverse.
